case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a plaintiff who owns a certified Title III Helms‑Burton “claim” to confiscated property may sue for “trafficking” when the defendant’s post‑confiscation commercial use occurs after the plaintiff’s confiscated property interest (allegedly a time‑limited usufruct/leasehold) would have expired, and whether Title III’s cause of action turns on the certified claim’s described property interest or instead on broader notions of the confiscated asset as a whole.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms‑Burton Act), 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A) (civil remedy for U.S. nationals who own claims to confiscated property against any person who “traffics in” such property), with related definitional provisions in § 6023 (definitions, including “confiscated” and “traffics”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Havana Docks argues that Title III creates a straightforward ownership-and-trafficking regime: if a U.S. national owns a certified claim to confiscated property (here, Havana’s dock and related facilities/rights as certified by the FCSC), then any later commercial use of that property by cruise lines constitutes “trafficking” regardless of arguments that the underlying confiscated interest was temporally limited. Petitioner emphasizes that the FCSC certification defines the relevant confiscated property interest and that the district court found Havana’s usufruct conferred plenary commercial control over the docks (not cargo-only), so defendants’ use of the docks for cruise operations trafficked in the very property identified in the certified claim. Petitioner (supported by the United States) also stresses Congress’s foreign-policy purpose: Title III is meant to deter private actors from enriching the Cuban regime through expropriated assets and to provide effective redress; importing an ‘expiration’ limitation would narrow Title III in a way Congress did not write and would undermine deterrence by allowing trafficking once a confiscated lease term would have run.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The cruise-line respondents argue that Title III liability must be tethered to the nature and scope of the property interest that was actually confiscated and owned by the plaintiff. If Havana’s confiscated right was a time-limited usufruct/leasehold, respondents contend that once that temporal interest would have ended, defendants cannot be trafficking in that interest because it no longer exists; at most they are using the underlying Cuban property, not the plaintiff’s former leasehold. Respondents warn that petitioner’s reading produces unfair and statutorily anomalous results, including potentially massive and duplicative recoveries untethered to the plaintiff’s actual confiscated interest (multiple recoveries by different interest-holders; liability for use decades after a limited-term interest would have expired). They frame Title III as effectively substituting the trafficker for the Cuban state as a “payor” of compensation for the specific confiscated property interest, so the statute should not transform confiscated property into perpetual ‘kryptonite’ forbidding all later commercial contact irrespective of the limited interest taken.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor press the best textual objection: § 6083’s “that interest” and the phrase “such property” can be read to confine the cause of action to the temporal scope of the confiscated leasehold/usufruct, so later uses are not trafficking in the plaintiff’s stick in the bundle. But even on that premise, § 6082(a)(1) asks whether the plaintiff presently owns a claim to confiscated property and whether the defendant traffics in confiscated property, and Congress defined “confiscated” to persist until return, compensation, or settlement—leaving no textual room for a court-created “would-have-expired” element as a categorical liability bar. As Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas note, § 6083(a)(1) makes certification conclusive proof of ownership of the certified interest, and importing counterfactual foreign-law expiration fights Congress’s administrability choice; the better minimalist course is to reject the Eleventh Circuit’s categorical expiration rule and remand to apply the statutory elements, while ensuring (per Sotomayor’s Gen. Motors fairness concern) that remedies are tethered to the certified interest’s scope and value. This approach avoids expanding Title III beyond the certified claim while also avoiding rewriting the liability elements to add an expiration defense Congress did not enact.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor press the best textual point: § 6083’s “that interest” and Title III’s references to “such property” suggest liability should track the scope of the certified leasehold/usufruct rather than the underlying asset in perpetuity. But nothing in § 6082(a)(1)(A) makes liability turn on a counterfactual “would-have-expired” inquiry; it turns on whether the plaintiff presently “owns the claim to such property,” and Congress made FCSC certification “conclusive proof of ownership” of that claim, foreclosing courts from adding an extra temporal element not enacted. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett note, § 6023(4)’s definition of “confiscated” as continuing until return/compensation/settlement is incompatible with reading in an implied cutoff based on how long the pre-confiscation interest might have lasted, though the time-limited nature of the certified interest can appropriately constrain valuation and damages. Justice Sotomayor’s Gen. Motors fairness concern may inform remedial limits, but under a strict textualist approach it cannot justify rewriting the liability trigger.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor press the best textual point: § 6083’s certification is conclusive only as to “that interest,” and “such property” can mean a bounded leasehold/usufruct rather than the asset in gross. But their proposed “would-have-expired” cutoff still asks us to add an extra element nowhere in § 6082 and to adjudicate counterfactual foreign-law term expiration despite Congress’s design—especially § 6083(a)(1)’s conclusive-proof rule—aimed at avoiding precisely that relitigation. As the Chief Justice notes, the Gen. Motors “no more than what was taken” intuition (raised by Justice Sotomayor) is better implemented through measuring damages to the certified interest’s value than by creating a categorical defense that would invite evasion and undermine Title III’s deterrent scheme. I therefore favor the Chief’s administrable approach: reject the Eleventh Circuit’s expiration rule and remand to apply the statutory elements using the certified interest as the benchmark, with any term-limits handled at remedies.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan press the strongest point that § 6083 makes FCSC certification conclusive and that § 6023(4)’s definition of “confiscated” persists until return/compensation/settlement, suggesting no textual room for a “would-have-expired” bar. But Justice Gorsuch is right to separate “ownership of the claim” from what “such property” is: § 6083’s conclusiveness attaches only to “that interest,” and Congress’s express inclusion of leaseholds/usufructs in § 6023(12)(A) indicates liability must track the bounded stick confiscated, not the underlying asset in gross. Shifting the term-limit problem to damages, as Roberts proposes, risks imposing liability untethered to any ongoing use of the plaintiff’s certified interest once it would have ended—an overbroad construction of a liability-creating statute that, on my pragmatic reading, would generate outsized, duplicative exposure beyond the real-world harm Congress targeted. The opposing side’s administrability concern is real, but it cannot justify reading “such property/that interest” to mean “the physical asset forever,” and I therefore stay with respondent.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor press the best textual-fairness point: “such property” and “that interest” should prevent a time-limited leasehold/usufruct from turning into a perpetual suit tethered to the physical asset. But I do not see that concern as justifying an extra-statutory “would-have-expired” element at the liability stage when § 6082(a)(1)(A) keys suit to who “owns the claim,” and § 6083(a)(1) makes FCSC certification conclusive proof of ownership of the certified interest—strongly signaling Congress wanted to avoid relitigating decades-old foreign-law expiration and renewal contingencies. Gen. Motors, as Justice Sotomayor invokes it, reinforces “no more than what was taken,” yet that principle fits the remedial/valuation inquiry (what is the certified interest worth, given its temporal limits) rather than a categorical bar that would let trafficking become lawful merely because time passed. Like the Chief Justice’s approach, I would reverse the Eleventh Circuit’s expiration rule and remand with the instruction that the certified interest cabins damages, not the existence of liability.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I appreciate the Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s point that § 6082 speaks in terms of ownership of a “claim” and that § 6083 makes FCSC certification conclusive proof of ownership of “that interest,” minimizing relitigation. But that conclusive-proof rule answers only who owns what was certified; it does not expand the certified, time-limited stick into the entire res for all time, and § 6082’s “traffics in such property” most naturally refers back to the same “interest” the plaintiff owns a claim to—especially given Congress’s express inclusion of leaseholds/usufructs in the definition of “property.” As Justice Sotomayor emphasizes, treating later use of the underlying asset as trafficking in an expired leasehold untethers liability from the confiscated interest itself; moving that mismatch to “damages” (as the Chief proposes) still presupposes liability for conduct that is no longer use of the plaintiff’s certified interest. Because Title III is liability-creating and the text is at best ambiguous on whether “such property” means the underlying asset in gross versus the certified interest, I would adhere to the narrower, interest-tracking reading rather than add breadth Congress did not clearly enact.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Gorsuch make the best textual/fairness point: § 6083’s “that interest” and Title III’s recognition of leaseholds/usufructs caution against treating a time-limited estate as a perpetual res. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that the Eleventh Circuit’s categorical “would-have-expired” bar is extra-textual and in tension with Congress’s claim-based design: § 6082 asks whether the plaintiff owns the claim and whether the defendant traffics in “confiscated property,” and § 6023(4) defines “confiscated” to persist until return/compensation/settlement, not until a hypothetical term end. The proper way to honor “that interest” is at the benchmark/valuation stage—using the certified claim’s described interest to limit what is recoverable—rather than nullifying liability once time passes, which would create an easy evasion channel inconsistent with Congress’s deterrent scheme. Institutionally and as a matter of administrability, importing counterfactual foreign-law expiration inquiries also risks the very uncertainty § 6083’s conclusive-proof rule was meant to avoid.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s textual point that § 6083(a)(1) is conclusive only as to “that interest” is the best argument for respondents, because it properly resists converting a time-limited leasehold into ownership of the whole res. But even taking that limit seriously, nothing in § 6082’s liability elements adds a counterfactual “would-have-expired” cutoff; instead, Congress defined “confiscated” to persist until return, compensation, or settlement, § 6023(4)(A), which indicates the actionable status turns on the unsatisfied claim, not a hypothetical term end. Justice Sotomayor’s General Motors-style concern about disproportionate recovery is real, yet under a textualist approach it fits at damages/valuation (as the Chief Justice suggests) by cabining recovery to the certified interest’s value, rather than by judicially creating an extra-statutory defense that defeats liability altogether. On that reading, we can respect “that interest” without rewriting Title III’s trigger away from trafficking in “confiscated property” tied to a certified, still-unsatisfied claim.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor press a serious textual/fairness concern: Title III’s repeated references to “such property” and § 6083’s “that interest” suggest liability should track the bounded, time-limited stick that was certified, not convert it into an effectively perpetual entitlement. But I remain persuaded that Congress chose an administrable, claim-centered trigger—plaintiff “owns the claim to such property” and FCSC certification is “conclusive proof” of ownership of that interest (as the Chief and Justice Kagan emphasize)—and that importing a “would-have-expired” liability cutoff would force courts into precisely the decades-old, foreign-law counterfactual inquiries Congress sought to displace. Justice Sotomayor’s Gen. Motors analogy reinforces the principle that recovery should be tethered to the interest actually taken, yet under Title III that concern is best implemented through valuation and remedies keyed to the certified interest, not by grafting an extra-textual expiration defense that would create an easy evasion route for trafficking once time passes. On my pragmatic approach, the statute’s definition of “confiscated” as continuing until return/compensation/settlement supports allowing liability to attach when defendants commercially exploit confiscated property tied to an unsatisfied certified claim, while ensuring proportionality through damages rather than categorical nonliability.

John Roberts.reasoning: The best reading of Title III turns on whether the plaintiff “owns the claim to such property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), and Congress made FCSC certification “conclusive proof of ownership” of the certified interest, § 6083(a)(1), suggesting courts should not superimpose a counterfactual expiration rule that is not in the text. Title III defines liability by a defendant’s post-enactment “traffics in” conduct with respect to “confiscated property,” § 6023(13), and nothing in § 6082 conditions suit on the plaintiff’s continuing entitlement absent confiscation; temporal limits are more naturally addressed in valuation/damages rather than as an atextual bar to liability. A narrow disposition consistent with institutional restraint is to reverse the Eleventh Circuit’s categorical “would-have-expired” rule and remand for application of the statutory elements using the certified claim’s described interest as the benchmark. This approach also respects Congress’s expressed purpose to deter commercial exploitation of expropriated assets, see § 6081(11), without creating judge-made carveouts that could undermine the scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of Title III authorizes suit by “any United States national who owns the claim to such property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), and it makes an FCSC “certification of a claim” conclusive proof of “ownership of the claim,” 22 U.S.C. § 6083(a)(1), so the cause of action turns on claim-ownership rather than on whether the underlying interest would have expired absent the confiscation. Congress defined “property” broadly to include time-limited interests (including “leasehold interests”), 22 U.S.C. § 6023(12)(A), and it defined “confiscated” as a continuing status until the property is returned, compensated, or the claim is settled, 22 U.S.C. § 6023(4), which forecloses importing a judicially created temporal cutoff. Respondents’ approach would rewrite the statute by adding an expiration limitation Congress did not enact and would nullify Congress’s express inclusion of time-limited property interests within Title III’s remedial scheme.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of Title III keys liability to whether the plaintiff “owns the claim to such property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), and it directs courts to treat FCSC certification as “conclusive proof of ownership” of the certified interest, § 6083(a)(1), which strongly indicates Congress chose a claim-ownership regime rather than a counterfactual inquiry into whether the plaintiff would still hold the underlying leasehold but for expropriation. Nothing in the definition of “traffics,” § 6023(13), or elsewhere imposes an expiration carve-out pegged to the confiscated interest’s would-have-ended date; importing that limitation would add a major restriction Congress did not enact and would undermine the statute’s deterrent, law-enforcement-like function against commercial exploitation of expropriated assets. Respondents’ fairness and multiple-recovery concerns are policy arguments better addressed through Congress’s valuation and damages structure (including reliance on the certified claim amount) rather than by rewriting the cause of action to extinguish suits after a hypothetical term end. Accordingly, a defendant’s post-confiscation commercial use can constitute trafficking so long as the plaintiff owns a certified claim to the confiscated property interest identified by the Commission.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title III’s cause of action is limited to trafficking in the specific “property” the plaintiff owns a claim to, and Congress’s definition of “property” expressly includes discrete, bounded interests like “leasehold interest[s]” and other “contingent right[s],” 22 U.S.C. § 6023(12)(A), indicating that liability must track the nature and scope of the confiscated interest rather than treating the entire asset as a perpetual res. If Havana’s certified claim is to a time-limited usufruct/leasehold, then post-confiscation commercial use occurring only after that temporal interest would have expired is not trafficking in that confiscated interest, even if it involves the same physical docks, because the claimed right no longer exists as a property interest. That reading avoids anomalous and unfair outcomes—potentially indefinite, duplicative recoveries untethered to what was actually taken—while remaining faithful to basic property-law distinctions Congress incorporated into the statute. As this Court has emphasized in the takings context, compensation (and by analogy, a statutory remedy keyed to the interest taken) is owed “for what is taken, not more,” United States v. Gen. Motors Corp., 323 U.S. 373, 382 (1945).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title III’s cause of action is triggered when “any United States national who owns the claim to such property” sues a person who “traffics in such property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), and Congress reinforced that claim-centered regime by making an FCSC “certification of a claim to ownership” “conclusive proof of ownership of that interest,” § 6083(a)(1). Nothing in § 6082 conditions liability on whether the confiscated interest would have expired absent expropriation; that temporal feature may bear on valuation/damages, but the statute’s text asks whether the defendant trafficked in the “property which was confiscated,” not whether it trafficked in a still-live leasehold at the time of use. Respondents’ reading would add an extra-statutory “expiration” limitation and would complicate administration (courts would relitigate counterfactual end-dates decades later) in tension with Congress’s decision to make certifications conclusive and to create a workable deterrent to post-confiscation commercial exploitation. The better textual compromise is to treat certification as fixing the actionable confiscated interest for ownership purposes (§ 6083), while allowing the limited-term nature of that interest to be accounted for in damages rather than as a categorical bar to suit.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Title III authorizes suit only by a U.S. national who “owns the claim to such property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), and Congress separately made an FCSC certification “conclusive proof of ownership of an interest in property” only as to “that interest,” § 6083(a)(1); those textual limits tie the cause of action to the claimant’s particular confiscated property interest, not the physical asset in gross. Reading “such property” and “that interest” to mean the specific right confiscated avoids turning a time-limited usufruct/leasehold into a perpetual entitlement to sue long after the described interest would have ended—an atextual expansion inconsistent with ordinary property principles recognizing property as a bundle of defined rights. Because the statute is at least ambiguous on whether post-expiration use of the underlying asset constitutes “trafficking” in the plaintiff’s confiscated interest, the better reading is the narrower one anchored to the certified interest, and any residual uncertainty in this liability-creating regime counsels against expansive construction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The text of Title III focuses on whether a U.S. national “owns the claim to such property” and whether the defendant “traffics in such property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), with ownership of the claim conclusively established by the FCSC certification, § 6083(a)(1). The statute does not condition liability on whether the claimant’s confiscated estate would have expired absent the confiscation; instead, Congress defined “confiscated” status to persist until the property is returned, compensation is provided, or the claim is settled, § 6023(4)(A), which cuts against importing a judicially created temporal-expiration limit. Respondents’ fairness and multiple-recovery concerns are better addressed through the statute’s valuation/damages mechanisms and the practical limits of what the certified claim actually covers, rather than rewriting the cause of action to terminate when a leasehold might have ended. Given the foreign-policy-laden, deterrence-oriented structure Congress adopted, judicial restraint favors enforcing the claim-based regime Congress wrote, not adding an extra-statutory “expiration” defense.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The operative text makes liability turn on whether the plaintiff “owns the claim to such property” and whether the defendant “traffics in such property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), with “traffics” defined to include use or other commercial dealing in confiscated property without authorization from “any United States national who holds a claim to the property,” § 6023(13)(A). Nothing in Title III conditions the cause of action on the continuing existence, under foreign law, of the particular temporal contours of the pre-confiscation interest (e.g., a usufruct’s natural expiration); instead, Congress defined when property remains “confiscated” (until returned, compensated, or settled), § 6023(4)(A), and tied proof of claim ownership to the FCSC certification, § 6083(a)(1). Reading an implied “expiration” limitation into “traffics in such property” would add a condition Congress did not write and would sit uneasily with the statute’s structure, which channels disputes about the relevant property interest through certification while making trafficking turn on later commercial exploitation of the confiscated asset as claimed.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title III’s text ties both who may sue and what conduct is actionable to present ownership of a “claim to confiscated property,” not to a counterfactual inquiry into whether the plaintiff’s underlying interest would have expired absent expropriation. See 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A) (liability to a U.S. national who “owns the claim”), § 6083(a)(1) (FCSC certification as conclusive proof of claim ownership), and § 6023(4)(A) (property remains “confiscated” until returned/compensated/settled), which together indicate Congress created a statutory cause of action anchored to the certified claim and continuing while the claim is unsatisfied. As a matter of procedural fairness and administrability, allowing courts to relitigate temporal property-law limits would undermine Congress’s decision to make certification conclusive and would invite unpredictable, case-by-case disputes about foreign property regimes. Practical consequences also favor petitioner: respondents’ approach would create an easy evasion channel—trafficking becomes permissible once a seized lease term would have run—contrary to the deterrent and remedial purposes Congress articulated in § 6081(6)(B).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a Title III Helms–Burton plaintiff who owns a certified claim to confiscated Cuban property may sue “traffickers” for post-confiscation use of that property even if the plaintiff’s confiscated property interest was time-limited (e.g., a leasehold/usufruct) that would have expired absent the confiscation.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms–Burton Act), principally 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A) (civil liability for “any person” who “traffics in” confiscated property owned by a U.S. national who “owns the claim”), and related definitional/limitations provisions (including the Act’s definitions of “traffics” and “claim,” and provisions addressing certified claims through the Foreign Claims Settlement Commission).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Havana Docks argues that Title III’s text allows suit by any U.S. national who “owns the claim” to confiscated property against any person who “traffics” in that property, and that once the Cuban government confiscated Havana Docks’ dock-related property interests (as reflected in its FCSC-certified claim), those interests became unlawful for private actors to exploit without exposure to Title III liability. Petitioner maintains that respondents’ cruise operations at the Havana docks constitute trafficking in the very property interest identified in the certified claim; that the Eleventh Circuit improperly narrowed the certified claim by treating the interest as temporally self-expiring; and that Congress designed Title III to deter commercial exploitation of expropriated property and to provide an effective damages remedy independent of whether the Cuban regime’s confiscation also prevented contractual expiration. Petitioner also stresses that any concerns about valuation or multiple recoveries are handled through claim valuation and statutory structure, not by rewriting Title III’s ownership/trafficking triggers.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The cruise-line respondents contend that Title III ties liability to trafficking in the plaintiff’s confiscated property interest as defined by the certified claim, and that where the confiscated interest is inherently time-limited (like a leasehold/usufruct), the plaintiff cannot recover for trafficking occurring after that interest would have naturally ended. Respondents argue that petitioner’s reading turns confiscated property into permanent “kryptonite” (forever off-limits), creating unfair and potentially duplicative recoveries and untethering damages from the nature and duration of the plaintiff’s actual property rights. They maintain the Eleventh Circuit correctly treated temporal limits the same way as spatial limits: the certified claim defines what the plaintiff owned, and trafficking must be in that defined interest during its life; after expiration, the plaintiff no longer has an owned interest capable of being trafficked in for Title III purposes (even if the physical asset continues to be used).

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondents’ best argument—avoiding a windfall where a term interest would have expired—raises a genuine equity concern, but it cannot justify importing an extra-textual temporal cutoff at the liability stage when § 6082 turns on present ownership of the “claim” and trafficking in property that “was confiscated,” and § 6023(4)(A) defines that status as continuing until return/compensation/settlement. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability point is particularly persuasive under a minimalist approach: the Eleventh Circuit’s counterfactual-expiration inquiry invites speculative, decades-later reconstruction that Congress avoided by making FCSC certification “conclusive proof” of ownership of the certified interest under § 6083(a)(1). Consistent with Justice Kagan’s framing, we can reverse narrowly—rejecting only the added temporal bar—while leaving on remand disputes about the scope of the certified interest and damages valuation to address any overcompensation concern. That course best respects the statutory design and preserves institutional legitimacy by enforcing the scheme Congress enacted rather than refining it judicially.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondents’ windfall argument, while intuitively appealing, asks us to graft a counterfactual-expiration limitation onto Title III that Congress did not enact. Chief Justice Roberts is right that the operative text turns on whether the plaintiff presently “owns the claim” and whether the defendant “traffics” in property that “was confiscated,” and § 6083(a)(1) makes FCSC certification “conclusive proof” of ownership of the certified interest—foreclosing courts from re-litigating the claim’s continued existence by hypothesizing an unconfiscated timeline. The statutory definition of “confiscated,” persisting until return/compensation/settlement, confirms the cause of action is status-based, not dependent on speculative reconstruction decades later; as Justice Kavanaugh notes, any overcompensation concern belongs in valuation and damages, not an atextual liability cutoff. Under original public meaning and textualist method, we enforce the scheme Congress wrote even if it yields results some view as generous in particular cases.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondents’ windfall argument has force as a matter of policy: imposing liability decades after a term interest would have expired risks converting Title III into leverage untethered from any present possessory entitlement. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 6082 asks whether the plaintiff presently “owns the claim” and whether the defendant “traffics” in property that “was confiscated,” and § 6083(a)(1) makes FCSC certification “conclusive proof” of ownership—leaving no textual room for the Eleventh Circuit’s counterfactual-expiration cutoff. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability point is persuasive under a practical textualist approach: Congress chose a certification-centered trigger rather than inviting speculation about how long a foreign-law concession might have lasted, and any overcompensation concern is better handled through valuation/damages tied to the certified interest. I therefore would reverse the added temporal limitation while making clear on remand that damages must reflect the scope and duration of the certified interest, not an atextual merits bar to liability.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Respondents’ strongest point remains the anti-windfall concern—why impose liability for trafficking after a term interest would have expired—but that is a damages/valuation issue, not a threshold liability rewrite, especially where Congress defined “confiscated” as an ongoing status until return/compensation/settlement. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on § 6083(a)(1)’s “conclusive proof” is decisive for me: letting courts negate certified claims via counterfactual expiration inquiries would hollow out Congress’s chosen, access-to-justice-friendly evidentiary regime and invite speculative, decades-later litigation that disadvantages claimholders. Justice Kagan’s administrability point underscores the real-world harm of the Eleventh Circuit’s approach—turning Title III into an expensive hypothetical-title contest rather than a workable remedy and deterrent against trafficking. Fairness concerns can be handled by calibrating recovery to the certified interest’s scope, but they do not justify grafting an atextual temporal cutoff onto § 6082.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Respondents’ best argument—that “owns the claim” should be read to expire when the underlying term interest would have ended—has real equitable force, but it asks us to graft a counterfactual reversion-date cutoff onto a statute that instead uses administrable, status-based triggers. Chief Justice Roberts is right that § 6083(a)(1)’s “conclusive proof” directive and Congress’s certification-centered scheme are hard to reconcile with reopening the merits through decades-later speculation about hypothetical expirations, especially given § 6023(4)(A)’s definition of “confiscated” as continuing until return/compensation/settlement. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability point reinforces that Congress chose a workable rule (certified claim + trafficking) and left any windfall concern to valuation/damages tied to the scope of the certified interest, not an extra-textual liability bar. On a pragmatic textualist reading focused on coherence and workability, the Eleventh Circuit’s temporal-limits rule adds a condition Congress did not write and destabilizes the definitional structure of Title III.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondents’ best point remains the anti-windfall concern—Title III should not morph into a perpetual federal tort divorced from the life of a time-limited pre-confiscation interest. But as the Chief Justice explains, Congress keyed liability to whether the plaintiff presently “owns the claim” and made FCSC certification “conclusive proof of ownership” of the interest described, which leaves no textual room for courts to negate a certified claim by hypothesizing a counterfactual expiration date. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability point reinforces the same separation-of-powers worry: inviting judges to reconstruct decades-old term limits and contingent foreign-law scenarios adds an extra-statutory limitation Congress did not enact. Any legitimate concern about overcompensation can be handled, as Justice Barrett notes, in valuation and damages tied to the certified interest, not by inserting a liability cutoff that the statutory definitions (including “confiscated” persisting until return/compensation/settlement) do not contain.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondents’ best argument remains the anti-windfall concern that Title III liability should not extend beyond the counterfactual end date of a pre-confiscation term interest, but that limitation is not in the statute and would require courts to build an atextual temporal cutoff. Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability point is decisive for me: § 6083(a)(1) makes FCSC certification “conclusive proof” of ownership of the certified interest, and the Eleventh Circuit’s approach effectively reopens that certification by forcing speculative, decades-later reconstruction of expiration contingencies as a threshold to liability. Justice Thomas’s reliance on the statutory definition of “confiscated” persisting until return/compensation/settlement further confirms Congress keyed liability to certified-claim ownership plus ongoing trafficking, not hypothetical reversion dates. Any fairness concerns about overcompensation should be addressed through valuation and damages on remand (i.e., the scope/value of the certified interest), not by judicially adding a non-textual bar to suit.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondents’ counterfactual-expiration theory has intuitive equitable appeal, but it asks us to add a temporal-liability cutoff Congress did not enact in § 6082(a)(1)(A). As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Title III hinges on present ownership of the statutory “claim” (with FCSC certification as “conclusive proof” under § 6083(a)(1)) and on trafficking in property that “was confiscated,” while § 6023(4)(A) treats confiscation as a continuing status until return/compensation/settlement—text that is hard to reconcile with an implied expiration rule. Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability point reinforces that Congress chose a certification-centered trigger rather than decades-later speculation about hypothetical lease or concession endpoints, especially in a foreign-law context. Any windfall concern is better addressed through the scope of the certified interest and damages/valuation on remand, not by rewriting the liability element.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondents’ best anti-windfall point—that liability after a term interest would have expired creates an overbroad, quasi-perpetual entitlement—raises a serious fairness concern, but it does not justify importing a counterfactual expiration bar at the threshold when Congress instead built an administrable, certification-centered scheme. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, § 6083(a)(1)’s “conclusive proof” directive and Title III’s focus on present ownership of “the claim” would be substantially diluted if courts must litigate decades-old hypothetical expirations as a gatekeeping issue, especially given § 6023(4)(A)’s choice to treat “confiscated” as a continuing status until return/compensation/settlement. I agree with Justice Kavanaugh that the proper place to avoid overcompensation is valuation and damages tied to the certified interest’s scope, which preserves procedural fairness by keeping the liability trigger predictable and avoids satellite litigation over foreign-law contingencies. Nothing in colleagues’ discussion introduces a precedent or statutory hook that genuinely undermines this text-and-structure reading, so I remain with petitioner.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title III authorizes suit by “any United States national who owns the claim to [confiscated] property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), and it separately directs that an FCSC certification is “conclusive proof of ownership” of the confiscated interest described in the claim, § 6083(a)(1). That structure focuses the cause of action on ownership of the certified claim and the defendant’s trafficking in the confiscated property, not on whether the plaintiff’s pre-confiscation interest would have expired absent the taking; the time-limited nature of the interest is more naturally handled at valuation/damages than by imposing a nontextual temporal cutoff on liability. A narrow disposition reversing the Eleventh Circuit better preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering to the statutory text and the conclusive effect Congress assigned to FCSC certifications, while leaving open on remand any issues about the scope of the certified interest and proper measurement of damages. This approach also avoids creating an atextual limitation that Congress did not write into Title III, especially in a sensitive foreign-affairs statute where the Court should be reluctant to add constraints not found in the enacted scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The controlling text makes liability turn on whether the plaintiff "owns the claim to" confiscated property and whether the defendant "traffics" in that confiscated property, not on whether the plaintiff’s pre-confiscation property interest would have naturally expired decades later. See 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A) (cause of action for any U.S. national who "owns the claim"), and § 6083(a)(1) (FCSC certification conclusively establishes the claim), together with § 6023(4)(A) (property remains "confiscated" until returned/compensated/settled) and § 6023(13)(A) (trafficking turns in part on lack of authorization from the U.S. national holding the claim). Respondents’ temporal-limits rule would add an extra-statutory expiration date that Congress did not write and would dilute the Act’s deterrent scheme so long as Cuba continues to hold the property "confiscated" within the statutory definition. Whatever the original concession’s duration, Congress chose a federal remedy keyed to certified claim ownership and continuing confiscation, not to background-law reversion dates.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of Title III imposes liability on “any person” who “traffics in property which was confiscated by the Cuban Government” when a U.S. national “owns the claim to such property.” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A). Congress keyed the cause of action to present ownership of a “claim” (conclusively established for certified claims, see 22 U.S.C. § 6083(a)(1)), not to a counterfactual inquiry into whether a time-limited underlying interest would have expired absent confiscation; importing that limitation adds words to the statute and would arbitrarily exclude many certified claims (including leasehold-type interests) that Congress plainly contemplated. The Act’s definition of “confiscated” indicates the claim persists until return/settlement/compensation, 22 U.S.C. § 6023(4)(A), and the practical consequence of respondents’ rule would be to invite trafficking precisely when it becomes most lucrative—after enough time passes—undermining Congress’s deterrent scheme.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title III imposes liability on “any person” who “traffics in” confiscated property owned by a U.S. national who “owns the claim,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), and it makes an FCSC-certified claim “conclusive” proof of ownership of the confiscated property interest described, § 6083(a)(1). Nothing in the Act instructs courts to run a counterfactual world in which confiscation never occurred and then to cut off liability when a time-limited interest would have expired; instead, the Act defines “confiscated” property as remaining confiscated until returned, compensated, or settled, 22 U.S.C. § 6023(4)(A), which better fits Congress’s deterrent and remedial purpose to protect victims of expropriation, § 6081(6)(B). Respondents’ “temporal expiration” rule would substantially narrow Title III’s practical reach in ways that invite manipulation and undercut Congress’s chosen enforcement mechanism against commercial exploitation of wrongfully taken property, while valuation and statutory limits can address fairness concerns about windfalls or duplicative recovery. Given Title III’s design to provide an effective remedy and deter trafficking, I would hold that a certified claimant may sue for trafficking so long as the property remains confiscated, even if the original interest was time-limited.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title III makes liability turn on whether a U.S. national “owns the claim” and a defendant “traffics in” the “confiscated property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), with FCSC certification treated as “conclusive proof of ownership” of the certified interest, § 6083(a)(1). Nothing in that text imports an additional, judge-made cutoff keyed to the hypothetical natural expiration of a time-limited interest; instead, the Act’s structure assumes the claim persists until the confiscation is remedied—i.e., the property is “returned,” “compensation” is provided, or the claim is “settled,” § 6023(4)(A)—and it defines “traffics” by reference to use/benefit from confiscated property without authorization from a U.S. national who “holds a claim,” § 6023(13)(A). Respondents’ temporal-limits rule reads “owns the claim” as “would own the property today,” undermining Congress’s evident deterrent design and creating an unadministrable inquiry into counterfactual expiration rather than the administrable trigger Congress chose (certified claim + trafficking). Any fairness concerns about overrecovery are better handled through valuation and the statute’s damages framework, not by narrowing the cause of action beyond what the text and definitional provisions provide.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The statute asks whether a defendant “traffics in confiscated property” and whether the plaintiff “owns the claim” to that confiscated property, not whether the plaintiff would still possess the underlying time-limited estate today absent the confiscation. See 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A). Congress further made an FCSC “certification of a claim” “conclusive proof of ownership of an interest in property,” § 6083(a)(1), and defined “confiscated” to persist until the property is returned, compensated, or the claim is otherwise settled, 22 U.S.C. § 6023(4)(A)—text that fits a continuing cause of action so long as the property remains confiscated. Respondents’ expiration-by-counterfactual approach would add a limitation Congress did not write and would invite courts to hypothesize how long the Cuban regime would have honored private temporal limits, contrary to the Act’s design to deter post-confiscation commercial exploitation of confiscated property.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title III authorizes suit by “any United States national who owns the claim to such property” against anyone who “traffics in property which was confiscated,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), and it separately commands that an FCSC-certified claim is “conclusive proof of ownership of an interest in property,” § 6083(a)(1). On the most workable reading, the certification fixes that a compensable confiscation occurred and who owns the claim, while any built-in temporal limits on the pre-confiscation interest go to valuation and damages rather than to categorical foreclosure of post-confiscation trafficking liability (otherwise courts must reconstruct counterfactual expiration regimes decades later, undermining administrability and Congress’s deterrent design). Nothing in the statutory text expressly cuts off the cause of action when a confiscated leasehold or usufruct would have expired, and adopting that cutoff would effectively add a limitation Congress did not enact, contrary to judicial restraint and the statute’s certification-centered structure. Given § 6083’s conclusive-proof rule and § 6082’s focus on “owns the claim” rather than current possessory entitlement, I would reverse the Eleventh Circuit’s temporal-expiration limitation and allow the action to proceed with damages reflecting the time-limited nature of the underlying interest.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Title III imposes liability on “any person” who “traffics in property which was confiscated by the Cuban Government” where the plaintiff “owns the claim to such property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), and it makes FCSC certification conclusive proof of claim ownership, § 6083(a)(1). Nothing in § 6082 conditions the cause of action on whether the confiscated interest would have expired absent confiscation; instead the Act’s definition of “confiscated” focuses on whether the property has been “returned” or “compensation … provided” (or otherwise settled), 22 U.S.C. § 6023(4)(A), which indicates Congress chose a status-based trigger rather than one keyed to the natural termination of a term interest. Respondents’ temporal-limits theory imports an atextual expiration rule that Congress did not write and is better addressed, if at all, through the certified valuation of the claim and Title III’s built-in limitations rather than narrowing “traffics” or “owns the claim.” Methodological consistency with the statute’s text and structure therefore supports allowing suit for post-confiscation trafficking in the confiscated property identified in the certified claim, even if the underlying interest was time-limited.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title III’s trigger is not continuing ownership of the underlying Cuban property interest, but present ownership of “the claim to such property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), and Congress directed that an FCSC-certified claim is “conclusive proof of ownership of an interest in property” that was confiscated, 22 U.S.C. § 6083(a)(1). The Act’s structure treats confiscated property as remaining “confiscated” until returned/compensated/settled, 22 U.S.C. § 6023(4)(A), and defines trafficking to turn on use of confiscated property without authorization from “any United States national who holds a claim,” 22 U.S.C. § 6023(13)(A), which aligns with a regime aimed at deterring ongoing exploitation and providing a workable, administrable remedy keyed to certification. Reading an implied temporal-expiration limit into liability would invite collateral relitigation of hypothetical contract endings decades later, undermining procedural fairness and predictability, while concerns about windfall or multiple recoveries are better handled through Congress’s valuation/certification framework and damages limits rather than narrowing who may sue. On this record, respondents’ post-confiscation commercial use of the very property identified in the certified claim falls within Title III’s “traffics in” prohibition notwithstanding that the pre-confiscation interest may have been time-limited.
